notes.definition: The theory of evolution by natural selection was proposed by Charles Darwin, based on observations on a round-the-world expedition, years of experimentation and discussion, and developing knowledge of geology and fossils. He published it in On the Origin of Species in 1859.
explanation: Charles Darwin was a naturalist who sailed around the world on HMS Beagle between 1831 and 1836. On the voyage, including on the Galápagos Islands, he made detailed observations of plants, animals and fossils. He noticed that species on different islands were similar but showed differences suited to their particular environments, such as finches with different beak shapes. After returning, he spent many years experimenting (for example, on breeding pigeons and plants) and discussing his ideas with other scientists. His thinking was also linked to developing knowledge of geology and fossils, which suggested the Earth was very old and that life had changed over time.

From this work Darwin proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection. Its key ideas are: individual organisms within a particular species show a wide range of variation for a characteristic; individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully; and the characteristics that have enabled these individuals to survive are then passed on to the next generation. Over many generations this leads to changes in species.

Darwin published his ideas in On the Origin of Species in 1859. There was much controversy surrounding these revolutionary new ideas. The theory was only gradually accepted for three main reasons. First, it challenged the idea that God made all the animals and plants that live on Earth, which was the widely held belief at the time. Second, there was insufficient evidence at the time the theory was published to convince many scientists. Third, the mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until about 50 years after the theory was published, so Darwin could not explain how characteristics were passed on.

Other theories were put forward to explain how species change. The best known is that of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, a French scientist working before Darwin. Lamarck's theory was based mainly on the idea that changes that occur in an organism during its lifetime can be inherited (the inheritance of acquired characteristics). For example, he suggested giraffes stretched their necks to reach high leaves, their necks became slightly longer, and this longer neck was passed on to their offspring. We now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur, because changes acquired during life do not change the genes in the gametes.

Over time, the evidence for Darwin's theory grew. The discovery of genes and how they are inherited explained how variation arises and is passed on, and further evidence came from fossils and from observing evolution happening, for example in antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Today the theory of evolution by natural selection is widely accepted by scientists. The story shows how scientific ideas change: a new theory may be resisted at first, but it becomes accepted as more evidence supports it and as other discoveries explain its mechanism.
keyFacts: Darwin's theory came from observations on a round-the-world expedition (HMS Beagle, 1831 to 1836).
It was backed by years of experimentation and discussion, and linked to developing knowledge of geology and fossils.
Individuals in a species show a wide range of variation for a characteristic.
Individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully.
The characteristics that helped them survive are passed on to the next generation.
Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.
Acceptance was gradual: it challenged the idea that God made all living things; there was insufficient evidence; the mechanism of inheritance was not known until about 50 years later.
Lamarck's theory: changes that occur during an organism's lifetime can be inherited.
We now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur.

keyTerms.definition: The process by which individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed, passing those characteristics on.
The book Charles Darwin published in 1859 setting out his theory of evolution by natural selection.
Lamarck's theory that changes acquired by an organism during its lifetime can be inherited by its offspring.
A characteristic that develops during an organism's life because of use, disuse or the environment, such as bigger muscles; it is not inherited.
Differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species.
How characteristics are passed from parents to offspring; now known to be through genes on chromosomes, which was not understood in Darwin's time.
A scientific explanation supported by evidence, which can be tested and may be modified as new evidence is found.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a characteristic the Darwinian way
workedExamples.question: Explain, using Darwin's theory, why cheetahs are able to run fast.
steps: Ancestral cheetahs showed a wide range of variation in running speed.
Faster individuals caught more prey, so they were more likely to survive to breed successfully.
They passed on the characteristics for speed to their offspring.
Over many generations, the population became faster.
workedExamples.answer: Variation in speed; faster cheetahs survived and bred; speed was passed on; over many generations cheetahs became faster.

workedExamples.title: Comparing Lamarck and Darwin
workedExamples.question: How would Lamarck and Darwin each explain why wading birds have long legs?
steps: Lamarck: birds stretched their legs to keep their bodies dry in deeper water; their legs grew slightly longer during life; this acquired change was passed to offspring.
Darwin: birds varied in leg length; those with naturally longer legs could feed in deeper water and were more likely to survive and breed; they passed on long legs.
The key difference: Lamarck's idea relies on changes during life being inherited; Darwin's relies on existing variation and selection.
workedExamples.answer: Lamarck: acquired changes inherited. Darwin: natural variation plus survival and breeding of the best suited.

workedExamples.title: Working with dates
workedExamples.question: Darwin published his theory in 1859. The mechanism of inheritance was not known until about 50 years later. Around which year did this become known, and how many years after the Beagle voyage began (1831) was the book published?
workedExamples.answer: Around 1909 (the early twentieth century); 28 years after the voyage began.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think Darwin's theory was accepted immediately.
misconceptions.right: In fact it was only gradually accepted, because it challenged religious belief, there was insufficient evidence at the time, and the mechanism of inheritance was not known for about 50 years.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think Darwin explained evolution using genes.
misconceptions.right: In fact Darwin did not know about genes. He could not explain how variation arose or how characteristics were inherited; that came later.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think Lamarck's and Darwin's theories are the same because both describe species changing over time.
misconceptions.right: In fact Lamarck said changes acquired during life are inherited; Darwin said existing variation is acted on by natural selection.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that a 'theory' in science is just a guess.
misconceptions.right: In fact a scientific theory is an explanation supported by a large body of evidence. The theory of evolution is now widely accepted by scientists.

realWorld: Observing antibiotic resistance spreading in bacteria is a modern, real-time demonstration of the natural selection Darwin described.
Studies of Galápagos finches since the 1970s have measured beak sizes changing after droughts, supporting Darwin's ideas with data he could not collect himself.
The history of Darwin's theory is used as an example of how scientific ideas are tested, debated and eventually accepted as evidence builds up.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Biology only (not Combined Science Trilogy): Darwin's development of the theory of evolution by natural selection, the reasons it was only gradually accepted, and Lamarck's alternative theory.
examTips: Learn the three reasons the theory was gradually accepted; they are commonly asked as a 3-mark question.
When describing how Darwin developed his theory, mention observations on a round-the-world expedition, experimentation, discussion with other scientists, and knowledge of geology and fossils.
For Lamarck, use the phrase 'changes that occur during an organism's lifetime can be inherited', and state that we now know this cannot occur in the vast majority of cases.
Learn the date 1859 and the title On the Origin of Species.
In compare questions, write a sentence on each theory and make the difference explicit (existing variation and selection, versus acquired changes being inherited).
summary: Darwin developed his theory from observations on a world voyage, experiments, discussion and knowledge of geology and fossils.
Individuals in a species vary; the best suited survive to breed and pass on their characteristics.
On the Origin of Species was published in 1859 and caused controversy.
Acceptance was gradual: religious objections, insufficient evidence and unknown mechanism of inheritance.
Lamarck proposed that changes acquired during life are inherited.
We now know acquired changes are not inherited in the vast majority of cases.

questions.question: Which scientist proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection?
options: Gregor Mendel
Charles Darwin
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
Louis Pasteur
markScheme: 1 mark: Charles Darwin
questions.explanation: Darwin proposed natural selection. Mendel studied inheritance in pea plants, Lamarck proposed inheritance of acquired characteristics, and Pasteur worked on microorganisms.

questions.question: In which year was On the Origin of Species published?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1859
questions.explanation: Darwin published his book in 1859. 1831 is when the Beagle voyage began, and the mechanism of inheritance was understood about 50 years after 1859.

questions.question: Lamarck's theory was based mainly on which idea?
options: Changes that occur during an organism's lifetime can be inherited
Individuals best suited to the environment survive to breed
God created all living things in their present form
Genes are found on chromosomes
markScheme: 1 mark: changes during lifetime can be inherited
questions.explanation: Lamarck believed acquired characteristics were passed on. Survival of the best suited is Darwin's idea; genes were not known in Lamarck's time.

questions.question: Which of these did Darwin NOT use to develop his theory?
options: Observations on a round-the-world expedition
Knowledge of geology and fossils
Discussion with other scientists
Knowledge of genes and DNA
markScheme: 1 mark: knowledge of genes and DNA
questions.explanation: Genes and DNA were not understood in Darwin's time. He used observations, experiments, discussion, and knowledge of geology and fossils.

questions.question:
Darwin's theory was only gradually accepted.
Which is one reason for this?
options: Darwin had never travelled outside Britain
It challenged the idea that God made all the animals and plants on Earth
Scientists already understood genes and rejected his ideas
Lamarck had proved Darwin wrong
markScheme: 1 mark: it challenged the idea that God made all animals and plants
questions.explanation: Many people believed in divine creation. Darwin travelled widely, genes were not understood, and Lamarck had not disproved Darwin.

questions.question: Which statement about Lamarck's theory is correct today?
options: It is fully accepted by scientists
It explains the inheritance of genes
In the vast majority of cases the type of inheritance it describes cannot occur
It was published after Darwin's theory
markScheme: 1 mark: in the vast majority of cases this inheritance cannot occur
questions.explanation: We now know changes acquired during life do not alter the genes passed on in gametes. Lamarck's ideas came before Darwin's book.

questions.question: According to Darwin, which individuals are more likely to survive to breed successfully?
options: The largest individuals
Those that try hardest to change
The oldest individuals
Those with characteristics most suited to the environment
markScheme: 1 mark: those with characteristics most suited to the environment
questions.explanation: Natural selection favours the best suited, which is not always the largest or oldest. Trying to change is a Lamarckian idea.

questions.question:
A blacksmith develops strong arm muscles through his work.
Which statement correctly explains whether his children will inherit strong arms?
options: Yes, because characteristics gained by use are passed on, as Lamarck said
Yes, because muscle cells make gametes
No, because the change in his muscles does not change the genes in his gametes
No, because only mothers pass on characteristics
markScheme: 1 mark: no, the change does not alter the genes in the gametes
questions.explanation: Acquired characteristics are not inherited because they do not change the DNA in sperm or eggs. Gametes are made in the reproductive organs, not muscles. Both parents pass on genes.

questions.question: Why did the later discovery of how genes are inherited help Darwin's theory to be accepted?
options: It proved that God did not create life
It explained how variation arises and how characteristics are passed on
It showed that Lamarck was correct
It showed that species never change
markScheme: 1 mark: it explained how variation arises and how characteristics are passed on
questions.explanation: Darwin could not explain the mechanism of inheritance. Genetics provided it, removing one of the main objections to his theory.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the dates of Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle.
Calculate how many years the voyage lasted.
markScheme: 1 mark: 5

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a timeline of some events in Darwin's life.
Calculate the number of years between the start of the voyage on HMS Beagle and the publication of On the Origin of Species.
markScheme: 1 mark: 28
questions.explanation: From Figure 1, the voyage began in 1831 and the book was published in 1859. 1859 − 1831 = 28 years. This long gap reflects the years of experimentation and discussion that backed up his observations.

questions.question:
A scientist measured the beak depths of 5 finches on an island.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean beak depth.
markScheme: 1 mark: sum = 49.0 mm
questions.explanation: 9.2 + 9.8 + 10.1 + 9.5 + 10.4 = 49.0. Mean = 49.0 ÷ 5 = 9.8 mm. Variation like this is what Darwin said natural selection acts on.

questions.question:
After a drought, only large, hard seeds were available on an island.
Table 1 shows the mean beak depth of a finch population before and after the drought.
Calculate the percentage increase in mean beak depth.
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: increase = 0.5 mm; 0.5 ÷ 9.4 × 100
questions.explanation: 0.5 ÷ 9.4 = 0.0532; × 100 = 5.32%, which is 5.3% to 2 significant figures. Finches with deeper beaks could crack the hard seeds, so more survived to breed.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the results of two surveys of scientists' views on Darwin's theory.
Calculate the increase in the percentage of scientists accepting the theory between 1860 and 1900.
markScheme: 1 mark: increase = 70 − 12.5 = 57.5 (percentage points)
questions.explanation: Calculate each percentage from its own total: 12.5% and 70%. The increase is 57.5 percentage points, showing the gradual acceptance of the theory as evidence grew.

questions.question: Give the title of the book in which Darwin published his theory.
markScheme: 1 mark: On the Origin of Species
questions.explanation: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.

questions.question: Name the scientist who suggested that changes which occur during an organism's lifetime can be inherited.
markScheme: 1 mark: (Jean-Baptiste) Lamarck
questions.explanation: Lamarck's theory is known as the inheritance of acquired characteristics.

questions.question: Give two sources of evidence or ideas that Darwin used when developing his theory.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: observations on a round-the-world expedition; years of experimentation; discussion with other scientists; developing knowledge of geology; fossils (max 2)
questions.explanation: Darwin combined field observations with experiments, discussion and the developing sciences of geology and fossils.

questions.question: Give three reasons why Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection was only gradually accepted.
acceptedAnswers: challenged idea that God made all animals and plants
markScheme: 1 mark: it challenged the idea that God made all the animals and plants on Earth
1 mark: there was insufficient evidence at the time to convince many scientists
1 mark: the mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known (until about 50 years later)
questions.explanation: These are the three reasons named in the specification and are often examined together.

questions.question: Describe the main ideas of Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection.
acceptedAnswers: most suited more likely to survive
characteristics passed on to next generation
markScheme: 1 mark: individuals within a species show a wide range of variation for a characteristic
1 mark: individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully
1 mark: the characteristics that enabled them to survive are passed on to the next generation
questions.explanation: These three linked points summarise Darwin's theory.

questions.question:
Giraffes have long necks.
Use Lamarck's theory to explain why giraffes have long necks.
markScheme: 1 mark: giraffes stretched their necks (during their lives) to reach high leaves, so their necks became longer
1 mark: this longer neck was passed on to their offspring
questions.explanation: This is the classic Lamarckian explanation. It is now rejected because acquired changes are not inherited.

questions.question: Explain why scientists now reject Lamarck's theory.
acceptedAnswers: changes during lifetime not passed on
markScheme: 1 mark: changes that occur during an organism's lifetime do not change its genes/DNA (in its gametes)
1 mark: so in the vast majority of cases they cannot be inherited
questions.explanation: Only genetic information carried in gametes is inherited. For example, children of people with tattoos or trained muscles do not inherit them.

questions.question: Suggest why knowledge of geology and fossils helped Darwin to develop his theory.
markScheme: 1 mark: geology suggested the Earth was very old, giving enough time for slow change over many generations
1 mark: fossils showed that organisms in the past were different from those today / species have changed or become extinct
questions.explanation: Natural selection needs a very long time, and fossils provided evidence that life had changed.

questions.question:
Darwin observed that finches on different Galápagos islands had different beak shapes.
Figure 1 shows the heads of finches, A, B and C, from three different islands, and the main food on each island.
Explain how Darwin's theory accounts for the different beak shapes.
markScheme: 1 mark: there was variation in beak shape in the finch population(s)
1 mark: different islands had different food sources, so finches with beaks best suited to the food on their island were more likely to survive and breed
1 mark: they passed on their beak characteristics, so over many generations each island's population developed a different beak shape
questions.explanation: Different environments select different characteristics from the existing variation.

questions.question:
The theory of evolution by natural selection was controversial in 1859.
Explain why the theory is now widely accepted.
markScheme: 1 mark: the mechanism of inheritance is now known (genes), explaining how variation arises and is passed on
1 mark: much more evidence has been collected, e.g. fossils, observed evolution such as antibiotic-resistant bacteria
questions.explanation: Scientific theories become accepted as evidence builds up and gaps in explanation are filled.

questions.question: Compare Lamarck's theory and Darwin's theory of how species change over time.
markScheme: Indicative content: both theories try to explain how species change over time; Lamarck: changes occurring during an organism's lifetime (through use or disuse) are inherited by offspring; Darwin: there is natural variation within a species; individuals most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed; their characteristics are passed on; Darwin's changes come from existing variation, not changes during life; Lamarck's type of inheritance cannot occur in the vast majority of cases; Darwin's theory is now widely accepted.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear comparison that describes both theories and states the key difference (acquired changes inherited versus selection of existing variation).
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes one theory, or both without a clear comparison.
questions.explanation: A comparison needs points about both theories and linking words such as 'whereas'. The key difference is where the change comes from.

questions.question:
Describe how Charles Darwin developed his theory of evolution by natural selection.
Explain why the theory was controversial and only gradually accepted.
markScheme: Indicative content. Development: observations on a round-the-world expedition (HMS Beagle), e.g. Galápagos finches and other species; years of experimentation; discussion with other scientists; linked to developing knowledge of geology (age of Earth) and fossils (life has changed). Theory: individuals within a species show a wide range of variation; those with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully; these characteristics are passed on to the next generation. Published in On the Origin of Species, 1859. Controversy and gradual acceptance: challenged the idea that God made all the animals and plants on Earth; insufficient evidence at the time to convince many scientists; mechanism of inheritance and variation not known until about 50 years later. Later discoveries in genetics and further evidence led to wide acceptance.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed and well-organised account of how the theory was developed, a clear statement of the theory, and all three reasons for gradual acceptance.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes some of how the theory was developed or the theory itself, and gives at least two reasons for gradual acceptance.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about Darwin's voyage or the theory, with little explanation of the controversy.
questions.explanation: A top answer covers three parts: how Darwin gathered evidence, what the theory says, and the three reasons for slow acceptance, ending with why it is accepted now.
